title: Reasons Why You Must Plan Your Finances
summary: Learn how to make your first financial plan: list what you own and owe, set goals with dates, and see a worked one-page example.
body_markdown:
Financial planning means writing down where your money stands, what you want it to do and by when, and what each goal needs every month. A first plan fits on one page. It takes an evening to draft, and after that you look at it once or twice a year.


## What is financial planning, and why does it matter?


Financial planning is deciding in advance what your money is for and when you will need it, then working out how to get there, instead of deciding one purchase at a time. A **financial plan** is the written answer: what you have and owe, what you want and by when, what each goal needs each month, and where each goal's money sits.


Planning covers your whole money life: spending, saving, debt, protection, tax and investing. **Investment planning** is one part of it. It decides where each goal's money is invested, based on when it is needed and how much risk can be taken.


A plan matters for three plain reasons.


- It shows how much of each month is already spoken for.
- It stops money you need soon from being put somewhere it can fall just before you need it.
- With emergency money set aside, one bad month is less likely to turn into a loan.


## How do you make a financial plan, step by step?


You make a first plan in six steps.


1. **List what you own and owe.** An **asset** is something you own that has money value, such as cash, deposits, investments, balances in EPF (Employees' Provident Fund, the retirement account salaried workers and their employers pay into each month) and PPF (Public Provident Fund, a government savings scheme with a 15-year account), property, gold or a vehicle. A **liability** is money you owe, such as loans and unpaid card bills. Your **net worth** is the total value of your assets minus everything you owe. It can be negative, for example early in a career with a large education loan. See[the four pillars of personal finance](https://koshex.com/blog/the-four-pillars-of-personal-finance) for a worked sheet.
2. **See where the month's money goes.** A **budget** is a plan for what you will spend and what you will keep aside each month. Our guide to[managing your money](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-money-management) shows how to build one. The[50-30-20 rule](https://koshex.com/blog/50-30-20-rule) is one common rule of thumb for splitting take-home pay, not a regulation.
3. **Set aside emergency money.** Emergency money is kept aside for sudden costs such as a job loss or a hospital bill. With it set aside, a sudden cost does not force you to sell investments when prices are low or stop your SIP. A **SIP** invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly. Three to six months of expenses is a common starting point, not a rule. A **fixed deposit (FD)** is money placed with a bank or company for a set period at a rate fixed when you open it. Read[where to keep emergency savings](https://koshex.com/blog/where-should-you-keep-your-emergency-savings) and[liquid funds versus fixed deposits](https://koshex.com/blog/liquid-funds-vs-fixed-deposits) before you choose a place.
4. **Write each goal with an amount and a date.** The next section shows how.
5. **Decide where each goal's money sits, by how soon you need it.** The money for a goal two years away has little time for a fall to recover before it is needed. The money for a goal thirty years away has time to sit through falls. The part of the plan that picks the investments is covered in[investment planning](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-investment-planning-and-why-is-it-important) .
6. **Review once or twice a year, and when life changes.** The last section covers what to check.


A loan costs you interest, and that cost is one factor in whether to repay it or invest. There is no single rule. Our guide to[getting out of a debt trap](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) covers repayment, and[prepaying a home loan or investing](https://koshex.com/blog/prepay-home-loan-or-invest) covers that particular choice.


## What should a financial plan include?


A plan should hold the same things SEBI makes a registered investment adviser ask a client before advising. Under regulation 16 of SEBI's Investment Advisers Regulations, the adviser must obtain the client's:


- age
- investment objectives, including how long they wish to stay invested and the purposes of the investment
- income details
- existing investments and assets
- risk appetite
- liability and borrowing details


SEBI's list is for advisers, not a duty on you to plan. It still makes a good checklist for your own plan. If you pay someone for a plan, our guide to[questions to ask a financial adviser](https://koshex.com/blog/5-important-questions-to-ask-your-financial-advisor) covers how to check their registration.


Add one more line for yourself: the dates on which you will review the plan.


The same regulation asks an adviser to assess the risk a client is willing and able to take, including their capacity for absorbing loss. In plain terms, **risk tolerance** is how big a fall you can sit through without selling, in money and in nerves. **Risk capacity** is how big a fall your finances can take without hurting a goal, given income, dependants, emergency money and time to the goal. Our guide to[risk tolerance](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-risk-tolerance-and-why-is-it-important) explains the difference.


Two housekeeping items belong in every plan.


- **Nominees.** A nominee is the person you name to receive the money if you die. Since 1 September 2026 you can name up to three nominees for a mutual fund (a pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager under SEBI rules) and say what share each gets. If you do not, they share equally. See[mutual fund nomination](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-nomination) .
- **KYC.** The mutual fund Investor Charter lists, among an investor's duties, keeping your KYC (identity and address) details updated: address, tax status, residency, PAN and bank account details. See[mutual fund KYC](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-kyc) .


Section 123 (the old Section 80C) allows a deduction of up to ₹1,50,000 a year in aggregate for individuals and Hindu Undivided Families, under the old tax regime only. The new regime applies unless you opt out. If you have no business income, you choose the old regime in your return each year, so file it by the due date. Our[tax-saving guide](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-save-tax-in-india-tax-saving-guide) and the guide to the[new tax regime](https://koshex.com/blog/features-of-the-new-tax-regime-and-its-benefits) go further.


## How do you set financial goals?


A goal is useful when it has an amount, a date and a monthly number. "Save for a course" is a wish. "₹1,44,000 in 24 months, which is ₹6,000 a month before any interest" is a goal.


Sort goals by how far away they are. A short goal is about three years away or less. The distance is your **time horizon** , how long until you need the money, and it drives step 5.


Some people check a goal against SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. It is a goal-setting checklist from management writing, and no regulator uses it.


To work backwards from a goal with a SIP, see[how much to invest in mutual funds every month](https://koshex.com/blog/how-much-should-i-invest-in-mutual-funds-every-month) .


## What does a first plan look like in practice?


Here is a one-page plan for Nidhi, 29, a lab technician in Bhopal. All the amounts are invented for illustration, and no return is assumed anywhere. Her take-home pay is ₹52,000 a month and her essential expenses are ₹28,000 a month. She has three goals: emergency money, a ₹1,44,000 professional certification course in two years, and retirement about 30 years away.


Equity means shares of companies. Debt means loans to governments, banks or companies, in the form of bonds, deposits and similar paper, so an FD sits on the debt side. Every mutual fund scheme must state an indicative time horizon (short, medium or long term) and carry a **riskometer** , SEBI's risk label on six levels from Low to Very High.


Goal Amount By when Each month Kept in


Emergency money ₹84,000 to ₹1,68,000 Build first A figure she chooses Savings account or fixed deposit


Certification course ₹1,44,000 2 years ₹6,000 Fixed deposit


Retirement Set with a calculator About 30 years Set with a calculator A long-term investment such as an equity mutual fund


The emergency range is ₹28,000 multiplied by three and by six, the common starting range. It is not a prescription.


The course money is ₹1,44,000 divided by 24 months, which is ₹6,000 a month. She keeps it away from equity because she needs it in two years. As a goal comes closer, there is less time for a fall to recover before you need the money. This is why some investors move money from equity towards debt in the last few years before a goal.


Her retirement money is 30 years from being needed, so it is the goal that can sit through falls. She works out the monthly figure with the[SIP calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/sip-calculator) , after reading about[when to start retirement planning](https://koshex.com/blog/best-time-to-start-retirement-planning) . You can browse[fixed deposits](https://koshex.com/fixed-deposit) and[mutual funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds) on the site.


The plan tells Nidhi what each rupee is for. The numbers are hers, not a template for yours.


## How do you plan on a salary, a single income or a tight budget?


The steps stay the same. What changes is the size of the buffer and how many goals run at once.


On a salary, the fixed pay date makes automatic transfers easy. Employer benefits such as EPF already count as long-term money, so check what yours holds. Our guide to[the Employees' Provident Fund](https://koshex.com/blog/employee-provident-fund-your-key-to-a-more-secure-and-stable-future) explains it.


With a single income or dependants, the buffer matters more.


With a small surplus, start with the buffer and one goal. A SIP can start small, as[micro-investing](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-micro-investing) and the guide to[systematic investment plans](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) show. Raising the SIP when income rises is one way to invest more over time, and[step-up SIPs](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) explains it.


## How often should you review your plan?


Review it once or twice a year, and whenever your income, your family or a goal changes. SEBI's investor site lists "periodically review" your portfolio among a smart investor's habits.


Check four things.


- Are the goals still the right ones, with the right dates?
- Is the emergency money still enough for your expenses today?
- Is each goal's money still matched to its date?
- Are your nominees still the people you want?


On the third check, your **asset allocation** is how your money is split between asset classes, such as equity, debt, gold and cash in the bank. **Rebalancing** is bringing your mix back to the split you chose after markets have moved it. See[how asset allocation affects a portfolio](https://koshex.com/blog/how-asset-allocation-impacts-your-portfolio) and[how to rebalance](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-rebalance-your-mutual-fund-portfolio) .


No one can reliably tell in advance when markets will rise or fall. A goal date is a reason to move money. A market level is not.


For a yearly checklist, see[money tasks for the start of the financial year](https://koshex.com/blog/things-to-do-at-the-start-of-the-financial-year) .
